newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss mechanical engineers support Holocaust fund.
newsitem.headline: Swiss mechanical engineers support Holocaust fund.

text.p: Swiss mechanical and electrical engineering companies pledged on Tuesday to support a Holocaust memorial fund that private businesses are financing as a humanitarian gesture to victims of Nazi persecution.

"Following the extended discussions in Switzerland and abroad, the reputation of Switzerland and its business community has been seriously tarnished," said Edwin Somm, president of the ASM/VSM machinery makers industry association.

"Our task must be to restore the good name of Switzerland and its business community," he told the group's annual news conference. He said companies in the sector planned a "substantial" contribution, but he was not more specific.
Separately, machinery company Georg Fischer AG said it was prepared to pay into the fund along with other companies in the sector, but did not indicate how much it would pay.

"Georg Fischer will take part in the Swiss humanitarian fund as an expression of its good will," it said, adding it was ready to help repair the image of Switzerland and Swiss business accused by critics of cynically profitting from World War Two.

Galavanised by international pressure and threats of losing business, big Swiss banks have already contributed 100 million Swiss francs ($68.5 million) to the fund, which is being coordinated by the Swiss government in Berne.

Berne is awaiting the first findings of a historians panel probing Switzerland's wartime role as a financial centre before deciding how to make amends for economic collaboration with the Nazis and its anti-Jewish refugee policy during the war.

Somm defended Swiss companies for conducting business with Nazi Germany, saying they were only following trade policy laid out by the government and parliament and which was in line with international law allowing neutrals to trade with belligerents.

"The shipments left our country with the authorisation of the authorities and they helped Switzerland supply itself with coal, food and other essentials," he said, adding this helped spare the country from invasion and destruction.

"But there was a negative side to to this strategy of survival -- the refugee policy, for example -- and Switzerland has good cause to show its gratitude," he said, especially for the fact its infrastructure survived the war virtually intact.
